claims.text: High-entropy alloys can have varying compositions.
Incorporating machine-learning algorithms, specifically neural networks, could improve the accuracy of melting-temperature prediction for high-entropy alloys.
Incorporating machine-learning algorithms could make prediction of melting properties in high-entropy alloys more computationally efficient.
The proposed intervention is to incorporate machine-learning algorithms into property prediction.
The intervention depends on the availability and use of existing datasets containing high-entropy-alloy properties and melting points.
Interactions among multiple principal elements in high-entropy alloys are composition-dependent and structurally consequential.
In AlxCrCoFeNi, changing Al content changes the stable FCC/BCC phase configuration.
Machine-learning models can learn patterns from existing high-entropy-alloy data to predict melting properties.
The proposed models will outperform traditional methods in predictive accuracy.
The proposed models will outperform traditional methods in computational efficiency.
Combined modeling and experiments can agree for a refractory high-entropy-alloy system and can support rapid assessment of other alloys.
First-principles calculations can predict composition-dependent phase stability in AlxCrCoFeNi with trends similar to experiment.
The validity of the proposed approach is limited by data quality.
The validity of the proposed approach is limited by data availability.
The validity of the proposed approach is limited by computational resources.
Machine-learning models may contain biases and therefore require extensive validation.
The hypothesis can be tested by comparing machine-learning predictions with experimental measurements for a set of high-entropy alloys.
The proposed benchmark will measure melting temperature, microstructure, and thermal stability.
A significant deviation between machine-learning predictions and experimental results would falsify the hypothesis.
